summary.text: Auxiliary weights \(u_k=k c_k\) are shown nonnegative by strong induction from the odd/even recursion for \(c_k\), using the bound \(c_k\ge 2^{k-1}/k\); hence the recursively defined prime-power coefficients \(b_e=\frac1e\sum_{k=1}^e u_k b_{e-k}\) are nonnegative.  The identity \(A005187(e)=e+A005187(\lfloor e/2\rfloor)\) yields that the Cauchy square of \((b_e)\) is \(2^{A005187(e)}\), so multiplicativity identifies the desired function with the product of these nonnegative prime-power coefficients.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 B(e):=\sum_{r\ge 0}\left\lfloor\frac{e}{2^r}\right\rfloor
 \qquad(e\ge 0).
\]
This sum is finite, since its terms vanish once \(2^r>e\). Thus \(B\) is A005187. Define the multiplicative function \(A\) by
\[
 A(0)=0,\qquad
 A(n)=\prod_{p^e\parallel n}2^{B(e)}\quad(n\ge1).
\]
This is A046644. The rational sequence whose numerator is A317940 is the Dirichlet-convolution square root \(f\) normalized by \(f(1)=1\). Equivalently, it is recursively given by
\[
 f(0)=0,	f(1)=1,
\]
and, for \(n>1\),
\[
 f(n)=\frac12\left(A(n)-
 \sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\1<d<n}}f(d)f(n/d)\right). \tag{1}
\]
We shall prove that \(f(n)\ge0\) for every \(n\ge1\).

The proof first constructs the required nonnegative coefficients locally, at a single prime.

### 1. Two elementary recurrences

The first recurrence is
\[
 B(0)=0,	 B(e)=e+B(\lfloor e/2\rfloor)\quad(e\ge1). \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, the term with \(r=0\) in the definition of \(B(e)\) is \(e\), while for \(r\ge1\),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{e}{2^r}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor e/2\rfloor}{2^{r-1}}\right\rfloor.
\]
Consequently, if we put
\[
 b_e:=2^{B(e)},
\]
then \(b_0=1\), and (2) gives
\[
 b_{2m}=2^{2m}b_m \quad(m\ge1),
 \qquad
 b_{2m+1}=2^{2m+1}b_m \quad(m\ge0). \tag{3}
\]

We next define rational numbers \(c_e\). Set \(c_0=0\), and for \(e\ge1\) define them recursively by
\[
 c_e=
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle \frac{2^{e-1}}e,&e\text{ odd},\\[6pt]
 \displaystyle 4^m\left(c_m-\frac1{4m}\right),&e=2m\text{ even}.
 \end{cases} \tag{4}
\]
The recursion is well-defined because in the even case \(m<2m=e\). Put
\[
 u_e:=e c_e. \tag{5}
\]
From (4) we immediately obtain the useful parity formulas
\[
 u_{2j+1}=4^j \quad(j\ge0), \tag{6}
\]
and
\[
 u_{2j}=2\,4^j u_j-\frac12\,4^j \quad(j\ge1). \tag{7}
\]
For (7), simply multiply the even clause in (4) by \(2j\) and use \(u_j=jc_j\):
\[
 u_{2j}=2j4^j\left(c_j-\frac1{4j}\right)
 =2\,4^j u_j-\frac12\,4^j.
\]

### 2. Positivity of the auxiliary coefficients

We claim that, for every \(e\ge1\),
\[
 c_e\ge \frac{2^{e-1}}e. \tag{8}
\]
We prove this by strong induction on \(e\). If \(e\) is odd, equality holds by definition. Suppose that \(e=2m\) is even, where \(m\ge1\). By the induction hypothesis,
\[
 c_m\ge \frac{2^{m-1}}m.
\]
Using (4), and noting that \(4^m>0\), we get
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 c_{2m}
 &=4^m\left(c_m-\frac1{4m}\right)\\
 &\ge 4^m\frac{2^{m-1}}m-\frac{4^m}{4m}\\
 &=\frac{2^{3m-1}-2^{2m-2}}m.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The desired lower bound at \(2m\) is
\[
 \frac{2^{2m-1}}{2m}=\frac{2^{2m-2}}m.
\]
Thus it remains only to observe that
\[
 2^{3m-1}-2^{2m-2}\ge 2^{2m-2},
\]
or equivalently
\[
 2^{3m-1}\ge 2^{2m-1},
\]
which follows from \(3m-1\ge2m-1\). This proves (8).

In particular, \(c_e>0\) for every \(e\ge1\), and hence
\[
 u_e=e c_e\ge0 \quad(e\ge1). \tag{9}
\]
This nonnegativity is the reason for introducing the sequence \(u_e\).

### 3. A recurrence satisfied by \(b_e=2^{B(e)}\)

We now prove the central identity
\[
 e b_e=2\sum_{k=1}^e u_k b_{e-k}
 \quad(e\ge1). \tag{10}
\]
Write
\[
 T_e:=\sum_{k=1}^e u_kb_{e-k}.
\]
We prove (10), equivalently \(T_e=e b_e/2\), by strong induction on \(e\).

For \(e=1\), formulas (6) and \(b_0=1\) give \(u_1=1\), so
\[
 2T_1=2u_1b_0=2=b_1=1\cdot b_1,
\]
because \(B(1)=1\).

Now suppose \(e\ge2\), and put \(m=\lfloor e/2\rfloor\), so \(m\ge1\). We split the sum defining \(T_e\) into its odd and even indices.

First let \(e=2m+1\). For an odd index \(k=2j+1\), where \(0\le j\le m\), equations (3) and (6) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 u_{2j+1}b_{2m+1-(2j+1)}
 &=4^j b_{2(m-j)}\\
 &=2^{2j}\,2^{2(m-j)}b_{m-j}\\
 &=2^{2m}b_{m-j}. \tag{11}
 \end{aligned}
\]
For an even index \(k=2j\), where \(1\le j\le m\), equations (3) and (7) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 u_{2j}b_{2m+1-2j}
 &=\left(2\,4^j u_j-\frac12\,4^j\right)b_{2(m-j)+1}\\
 &=\left(2\,2^{2j}u_j-\frac12\,2^{2j}\right)
       2^{2(m-j)+1}b_{m-j}\\
 &=4\,2^{2m}u_jb_{m-j}-2^{2m}b_{m-j}. \tag{12}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Summing (11) and (12), we obtain
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 T_{2m+1}
 &=2^{2m}\sum_{j=0}^m b_{m-j}
   +4\,2^{2m}\sum_{j=1}^m u_jb_{m-j}
   -2^{2m}\sum_{j=1}^m b_{m-j}\\
 &=2^{2m}\bigl(b_m+4T_m\bigr). \tag{13}
 \end{aligned}
\]
By the induction hypothesis, \(T_m=mb_m/2\). Hence
\[
 T_{2m+1}=2^{2m}(1+2m)b_m.
\]
Using \(b_{2m+1}=2^{2m+1}b_m\) from (3), this is exactly
\[
 T_{2m+1}=\frac{(2m+1)b_{2m+1}}2.
\]

Now let \(e=2m\). For odd indices \(k=2j+1\), with \(0\le j<m\), we similarly have
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 u_{2j+1}b_{2m-(2j+1)}
 &=4^j b_{2(m-1-j)+1}\\
 &=2^{2m-1}b_{m-1-j}. \tag{14}
 \end{aligned}
\]
For even indices \(k=2j\), with \(1\le j\le m\), we get
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 u_{2j}b_{2m-2j}
 &=\left(2\,4^ju_j-\frac12\,4^j\right)b_{2(m-j)}\\
 &=4\,2^{2m-1}u_jb_{m-j}
   -2^{2m-1}b_{m-j}. \tag{15}
 \end{aligned}
\]
The two unweighted sums occurring after (14) and (15) are equal, since
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{m-1}b_{m-1-j}=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}b_i
 =\sum_{j=1}^m b_{m-j}.
\]
They therefore cancel, leaving
\[
 T_{2m}=4\,2^{2m-1}\sum_{j=1}^m u_jb_{m-j}
       =4\,2^{2m-1}T_m.
\]
By induction this equals
\[
 4\,2^{2m-1}\frac{mb_m}{2}
 =m\,2^{2m}b_m.
\]
Since \(b_{2m}=2^{2m}b_m\), this is
\[
 T_{2m}=\frac{(2m)b_{2m}}2.
\]
Thus (10) holds in both parity cases.

### 4. Construction of nonnegative local square-root coefficients

Define rational numbers \(a_e\) recursively by
\[
 a_0=1,
 \qquad
 a_e=\frac1e\sum_{k=1}^e u_k a_{e-k}
 \quad(e\ge1). \tag{16}
\]
Every \(a_e\) is nonnegative. Indeed, this follows by strong induction. The initial value is \(a_0=1\). For \(e\ge1\), every \(u_k\) in (16) is nonnegative by (9), and every \(a_{e-k}\) is nonnegative by induction because \(e-k<e\). Thus the numerator in (16) is nonnegative; division by the positive integer \(e\) preserves nonnegativity. Therefore
\[
 a_e\ge0\quad\text{for all }e\ge0. \tag{17}
\]

We next show that the ordinary additive convolution square of \((a_e)\) is \((b_e)\). Define
\[
 S_e:=\sum_{j=0}^e a_j a_{e-j}. \tag{18}
\]
We first derive a recurrence for \(S_e\). For \(e\ge1\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 eS_e
 &=\sum_{j=0}^e \bigl(j+(e-j)\bigr)a_ja_{e-j}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Under the substitution \(j\mapsto e-j\), the sum involving the second summand \(e-j\) becomes the same as the sum involving \(j\). Hence
\[
 eS_e=2\sum_{j=0}^e j a_j a_{e-j}. \tag{19}
\]
Multiplying (16) by \(j\) gives, also for \(j=0\) since both sides then vanish,
\[
 j a_j=\sum_{k=1}^j u_k a_{j-k}. \tag{20}
\]
Substitute (20) into (19) and interchange the order of the two finite sums:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 eS_e
 &=2\sum_{j=0}^e\sum_{k=1}^j
     u_k a_{j-k}a_{e-j}\\
 &=2\sum_{k=1}^e u_k
     \sum_{j=k}^e a_{j-k}a_{e-j}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
In the inner sum put \(i=j-k\). Then \(0\le i\le e-k\), and
\[
 e-j=e-k-i.
\]
Thus the inner sum is exactly \(S_{e-k}\), proving
\[
 eS_e=2\sum_{k=1}^e u_kS_{e-k}. \tag{21}
\]

We can now compare (21) with (10). We claim
\[
 S_e=b_e=2^{B(e)}\quad(e\ge0). \tag{22}
\]
For \(e=0\), (18) gives \(S_0=a_0^2=1=b_0\). Suppose \(e\ge1\) and that (22) has already been proved for every smaller index. Then (21) and the induction hypothesis yield
\[
 eS_e=2\sum_{k=1}^e u_kb_{e-k}.
\]
By (10), the right side is \(eb_e\). Since \(e\ne0\), cancellation gives \(S_e=b_e\). This completes the induction and proves (22). In other words,
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^e a_ja_{e-j}=2^{B(e)} \quad(e\ge0). \tag{23}
\]

### 5. Assembly over all primes

For \(n\ge1\), with prime factorization
\[
 n=\prod_p p^{v_p(n)},
\]
define
\[
 \alpha(n):=\prod_p a_{v_p(n)}, \tag{24}
\]
where only the finitely many primes dividing \(n\) contribute; also set \(\alpha(0)=0\). Since \(a_0=1\), formula (24) gives \(\alpha(1)=1\). It also makes \(\alpha\) multiplicative: if \(x\) and \(y\) are coprime, their nonzero prime exponents have disjoint supports, and therefore
\[
 \alpha(xy)=\alpha(x)\alpha(y).
\]
Most importantly, (17) gives
\[
 \alpha(n)\ge0\quad(n\ge1), \tag{25}
\]
because it is a finite product of nonnegative rational numbers.

We claim that the Dirichlet convolution square of \(\alpha\) is \(A\):
\[
 (\alpha*\alpha)(n)=A(n). \tag{26}
\]
Both sides are multiplicative functions, so it is enough to compare them on prime powers. For a prime \(p\) and \(e\ge0\), the divisors of \(p^e\) are precisely \(p^j\), \(0\le j\le e\). Hence
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 (\alpha*\alpha)(p^e)
 &=\sum_{j=0}^e\alpha(p^j)\alpha(p^{e-j})\\
 &=\sum_{j=0}^e a_ja_{e-j}\\
 &=2^{B(e)}
 =A(p^e),
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the third equality is (23). To spell out why equality on prime powers suffices, if \(n=\prod_p p^{e_p}\), multiplicativity gives both sides at \(n\) as the product of their values at the finitely many prime powers \(p^{e_p}\). Thus (26) follows.

### 6. Identification with the recursively defined square root

It remains to show that \(\alpha\) is exactly the sequence \(f\) defined by (1). This follows either from uniqueness of a Dirichlet-convolution square root with value \(1\) at \(1\), or directly by strong induction; we give the direct argument.

At \(n=1\), both values are \(1\). Suppose \(n>1\), and assume \(f(m)=\alpha(m)\) for every positive \(m<n\). Expanding (26) at \(n\),
\[
 A(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\alpha(d)\alpha(n/d).
\]
The divisors \(d=1\) and \(d=n\) contribute
\[
 \alpha(1)\alpha(n)+\alpha(n)\alpha(1)=2\alpha(n).
\]
Every other divisor satisfies \(1<d<n\). Therefore
\[
 A(n)=2\alpha(n)+
 \sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\1<d<n}}
 \alpha(d)\alpha(n/d). \tag{27}
\]
For every divisor in the remaining sum, both \(d<n\) and \(n/d<n\): the latter follows from \(d>1\). The induction hypothesis therefore allows us to replace both factors by \(f\). Rearranging (27) gives
\[
 \alpha(n)=\frac12\left(A(n)-
 \sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\1<d<n}}f(d)f(n/d)\right).
\]
By the defining recurrence (1), the right side is \(f(n)\). Hence \(f(n)=\alpha(n)\), completing the induction.

Finally, (25) now yields
\[
 f(n)=\alpha(n)\ge0
 \qquad\text{for every }n\ge1.
\]
Since a nonnegative rational number has nonnegative numerator when written in lowest terms with positive denominator, the numerators forming A317940 are nonnegative as well. Thus, for every integer \(n\ge1\), \(a(n)\ge0\), as claimed.
